action_criteria.expected_evidence: Irregular, heterogeneously ring-enhancing right cerebellar hemisphere mass (3.2 x 4.1 x 3.5 cm) extending to the vermis, with a second 1.8 cm superior vermian enhancing lesion, central necrosis, intratumoral hemorrhage, peripheral restricted diffusion and edema, compressing the fourth ventricle with early obstructive hydrocephalus and transependymal CSF flow
action_criteria.label: Order MRI brain with and without gadolinium contrast (tumor protocol with DWI, FLAIR, post-contrast T1) to characterize the right cerebellar lesion, define the fourth-ventricle compression and hydrocephalus, and plan surgery
action_criteria.rationale: Contrast MRI characterizes the lesion, shows its relation to the fourth ventricle and brainstem, and plans the approach; it precedes any tissue sampling (EANO 2021).

action_criteria.rationale: Staging CT is optional here: metastasis is on the imaging differential of an adult posterior fossa mass, but there is no known primary and tissue is diagnostic.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Mild microcytic anemia (Hb 11.2 g/dL, MCV 76.5 fL) with normal platelets, coagulation and electrolytes and a negative beta-hCG: no contraindication to surgery

action_criteria.rationale: Platelets, coagulation, electrolytes and type and screen must be known before a neurosurgical procedure and before dexamethasone.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Integrated diagnosis Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, CNS WHO grade 4 with IDH1 R132H IHC negative, no IDH1/IDH2 mutation on sequencing, ATRX retained, H3 K27M not detected with H3K27me3 retained, and MGMT promoter methylated
action_criteria.label: Obtain tissue by maximal safe resection of the right cerebellar and vermian lesion, or stereotactic biopsy if resection is not safely feasible, for an integrated histomolecular diagnosis with IDH1 R132H immunohistochemistry, IDH1/IDH2 sequencing (age under 55), ATRX, H3 K27 status (vermian involvement) and MGMT promoter methylation
action_criteria.rationale: Surgery is the first option for a resectable glioma and should be as extensive as safely possible (AIOM; EANO 2021); here resection also relieves the fourth-ventricle compression. Only tissue establishes the integrated diagnosis and the molecular results that select treatment; EANO 2021 asks for IDH sequencing when IHC is negative under 55 years and H3 K27 status in gliomas involving the midline.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Methylation class glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype (RTK II), with no match to high-grade astrocytoma with piloid features or diffuse paediatric-type high-grade glioma
action_criteria.label: Add genome-wide DNA methylation profiling to the tissue work-up, because at 21 a cerebellar IDH- and H3-wildtype high-grade glioma may be a high-grade astrocytoma with piloid features or a diffuse paediatric-type high-grade glioma
action_criteria.rationale: A methylation profile is an essential criterion of both entities, which histology and the targeted assays do not exclude reliably in a young adult with a cerebellar tumour (WHO CNS5).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Estrogen-containing contraceptive adds thromboembolic risk to malignancy and surgery; sulfonamide allergy excludes trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for later Pneumocystis prophylaxis; no significant dexamethasone interaction
action_criteria.label: Check interactions of dexamethasone with the current medicines (combined oral contraceptive, ferrous sulfate, sumatriptan) and the sulfonamide allergy
action_criteria.rationale: Optional: no interaction changes the immediate diagnostic plan, but the contraceptive and the allergy matter for later treatment.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not perform a lumbar puncture: fourth-ventricle compression with obstructive hydrocephalus and papilledema carries a risk of tonsillar herniation.
Do not initiate definitive tumor-directed therapy (radiation, temozolomide, alkylating chemotherapy) before tissue diagnosis is established
Do not start therapeutic anticoagulation without a clear thromboembolic indication, given upcoming neurosurgical intervention and bleeding risk
Do not start prophylactic antiseizure medication: the patient has had no seizure, and AIOM recommends against prophylaxis in brain tumour patients without a seizure history.
required_recommendations: Refer urgently to neurosurgery for maximal safe resection of the right cerebellar and vermian lesion, with stereotactic biopsy if resection is not safely feasible; send the specimen for an integrated histomolecular diagnosis (WHO CNS5).

Manage the obstructive hydrocephalus with neurosurgery now: early posterior fossa resection to restore CSF flow, with an external ventricular drain or endoscopic third ventriculostomy if headache, vomiting or consciousness worsen before surgery, and close neurological observation in the meantime.

Start dexamethasone for symptomatic vasogenic oedema (for example 4 mg every 6 to 8 hours after a loading dose when mass effect is marked) at the lowest effective dose, with glucose monitoring and gastric protection, and taper after surgery.

Before oncological treatment, stop the estrogen-containing oral contraceptive (added venous thromboembolism risk with malignancy and surgery), arrange effective non-estrogen contraception because temozolomide is teratogenic, and offer fertility preservation counselling before chemoradiotherapy.

After the integrated diagnosis, refer to the neuro-oncology multidisciplinary team; for glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, at age 70 or under with KPS 70 or more, radiotherapy 60 Gy in 30 fractions with concomitant and adjuvant temozolomide (Stupp 2005; EANO 2021).

mri.impression: Two irregularly contoured, heterogeneously enhancing mass lesions involving the right cerebellar hemisphere and vermis with evidence of intratumoral hemorrhage, central necrosis, and surrounding edema. Compression of the fourth ventricle with early obstructive hydrocephalus and transependymal CSF flow. Imaging characteristics raise concern for a high-grade neoplasm. Given the posterior fossa location in a young patient, differential diagnosis includes primary high-grade glioma (glioblastoma), metastatic disease, ependymoma, medulloblastoma, and hemangioblastoma. The infiltrative margins and heterogeneous enhancement with necrosis favor a high-grade glial tumor. An incidental benign pineal cyst is also noted

patient.history_present_illness: This 21-year-old right-handed Hispanic woman presents with a two-month history of progressively worsening headaches, nausea, and vomiting. The headaches began insidiously approximately eight weeks ago, initially described as a dull, occipital pressure that she attributed to stress from her college coursework. Over the past month, the headaches have become more severe and persistent, now occurring daily, often waking her from sleep in the early morning hours. They are associated with nausea and non-bilious vomiting, which has worsened over the past two weeks to the point where she has difficulty keeping food down and has lost approximately 4 kg of body weight. She reports that her typical migraines feel different from these new headaches, noting the current ones are more diffuse, worse with Valsalva maneuvers, and do not respond to her usual sumatriptan. She also describes progressive difficulty with balance and coordination over the past six weeks. She first noticed clumsiness when handling objects and dropping her phone more frequently. Over the past month, she has had increasing difficulty walking, describing a sense of unsteadiness and veering to the right side. She had to stop playing recreational volleyball three weeks ago because she could no longer coordinate her movements effectively. Her roommate noted that her handwriting has become progressively more illegible. She denies any seizures, loss of consciousness, visual changes other than occasional blurred vision, hearing loss, weakness, numbness, or tingling. She has not had fevers, night sweats, weight loss beyond what she attributes to poor oral intake, or any recent infections. She has no history of trauma. Her family history is notable for breast and ovarian cancer on the maternal side, which has caused her significant anxiety.
